title: Periodizing the Postmodern
description: Where the term came from, and how it differs from poststructuralism

concepts.title: A Word Before It Was a Doctrine
concepts.contentHtml:
The word postmodern circulated for half a century before it congealed into a school. Arnold Toynbee, in A Study of History (vols. 1934–61), used "post-Modern" to mark the cultural rupture he located around 1875: the end of bourgeois rationalism and the onset of mass irrationalism. Architectural critics — Joseph Hudnut in 1945, then Charles Jencks in The Language of Post-Modern Architecture (1977) — used it for buildings that broke with the austere International Style by quoting historical ornament with knowing irony.

The philosophical sense, the one this topic studies, crystallized only with Jean-François Lyotard's La condition postmoderne (1979), commissioned by the Conseil des universités du Québec. Lyotard borrowed the term from sociology and aesthetics and transposed it into a thesis about knowledge.

Treat "postmodern" as a family-resemblance label, not a single doctrine. It names a constellation: a historical period, a set of artistic strategies, a stance toward truth. The constellation has a center of gravity, not a strict definition. The first task is to resist the urge to police the word — and the second is to notice that almost no thinker called "postmodern" willingly accepted the label.

concepts.title: Postmodernism vs. Poststructuralism
concepts.contentHtml:
The two terms are routinely confused, partly because their canons overlap. Sharpen the distinction this way:

Poststructuralism is a methodological-philosophical movement, mainly French, mainly the 1960s–70s. It begins from structuralism (Saussure, Lévi-Strauss) and undermines its faith in stable underlying systems: Derrida's différance, Foucault's genealogies of power/knowledge, Lacan's rereading of Freud, Deleuze and Guattari's rhizomes. Its problems are linguistic, semiotic, and epistemic.

Postmodernism is broader and shaggier: a diagnosis of a cultural-historical condition. Its problems are aesthetic (pastiche, the loss of the avant-garde), political-economic (consumer capitalism, media saturation), and epistemic (the legitimacy of grand narratives). It includes Anglo-American voices (Jameson, Rorty, Hutcheon) that poststructuralism doesn't.

The relationship is one of overlap, not equivalence. Lyotard, Baudrillard, and Derrida show up in both maps. But you can be a poststructuralist without diagnosing late capitalism (Derrida) and a postmodernist without doing semiotic theory (Jencks). Conflating them flattens both. This topic focuses on the cultural-epistemic strand; philosophy-poststructuralism covers the other.

concepts.title: Three Theses That Recur
concepts.contentHtml:
Beneath the diversity, three commitments recur often enough to count as the postmodern core.

(1) Anti-foundationalism. There is no neutral, theory-free standpoint — no "view from nowhere" — from which to ground knowledge, ethics, or aesthetics. Every supposed foundation (sense-data, the cogito, a priori categories, formal logic) is itself situated in a tradition, language, or practice.

(2) Incredulity toward metanarratives. Lyotard's signature line. Big stories that purport to legitimize knowledge or progress as a whole — Hegelian Spirit, Marxist emancipation, the Enlightenment's universal Reason, scientific positivism — have lost their grip. What remains is local, plural, and contestable.

(3) The collapse of depth models. Jameson's diagnosis: postmodern culture refuses the inside/outside, surface/depth, real/apparent dichotomies that organized modernist thought. Pastiche replaces parody; surfaces stop pointing to depths; the sign refers chiefly to other signs.

None of these is unique to postmodernism — Wittgenstein, Nietzsche, and the pragmatists got there first on (1) — but their combination, applied across philosophy, art, and politics, is what gives the postmodern its distinctive accent.

title: Lyotard and the Postmodern Condition
description: Metanarratives, language games, and paralogy as a new criterion of legitimation

concepts.title: Incredulity Toward Metanarratives
concepts.contentHtml:
Lyotard's The Postmodern Condition: A Report on Knowledge (1979) opens with one of the most quoted sentences in twentieth-century philosophy: "I define postmodern as incredulity toward metanarratives" (incrédulité à l'égard des métarécits).

A metanarrative (or grand récit) is a second-order story that legitimates first-order practices. Modernity ran on two principal ones, Lyotard argues: the narrative of emancipation (knowledge frees humanity, from the Enlightenment through Marxism) and the narrative of speculation (knowledge is the self-realization of Spirit, from Hegel through the German university). Both promise that local activities — this experiment, this revolution, this curriculum — gain meaning by participation in a universal story.

Lyotard's claim is sociological as much as philosophical: by the late 1970s, those stories no longer command belief. After the Gulags, after Hiroshima, after capital's absorption of the New Left, the metanarratives have become unusable. We continue to do science, art, and politics, but the umbrella has folded. The book is short, dense, and was originally a policy report — its tone is diagnostic, not celebratory.

concepts.title: Language Games and the Pragmatics of Knowledge
concepts.contentHtml:
What replaces metanarratives? Lyotard turns to Wittgenstein's notion of language games from the Philosophical Investigations. Knowledge, he argues, is not a single hierarchy but a multiplicity of games — denotative, prescriptive, narrative, technical — each with its own rules and criteria of admissible moves.

This pragmatic turn matters. Truth-claims belong to the denotative game; ethical claims to the prescriptive; mythic narratives to a third. The error of metanarrative thinking is to imagine that one game (typically the denotative-scientific) can adjudicate all the others. For Lyotard, no neutral metalanguage exists. The games are incommensurable; the most one can do is move between them, register the different stakes, and refuse the imperialism of any single criterion.

This pluralism is not relativism in the cheap sense. Lyotard insists that within a game, moves can be assessed; what is gone is the dream of a single criterion across games. The political consequence — taken up later in The Differend (1983) — is that injuries phrased in one game may be unspeakable in another, and the philosopher's job is to witness these differends rather than dissolve them with false synthesis.

concepts.title: Performativity and Paralogy
concepts.contentHtml:
Lyotard's most uncomfortable diagnosis concerns how scientific knowledge actually gets legitimated once the metanarratives fail. The default replacement, he argues, is performativity: the criterion that a research program is good if it improves the input/output ratio of the system — more papers, more grants, more applications, more capital. This is legitimation by efficiency, congenial to capital and to the bureaucratic state, and it quietly subordinates truth to power.

Against performativity, Lyotard proposes paralogy as the proper postmodern criterion. Paralogy (from Greek para-, beside, plus logos) means generative dissent: the production of new moves, new rules, new games — drawing implicitly on Kuhn's revolutionary science and on the open-ended formal results of Gödel and Mandelbrot. Knowledge advances by destabilizing consensus, not by optimizing it.

The proposal has been criticized as romantic — does paralogy not also need legitimation? — and its political implications remain contested. But the diagnosis of performativity has aged extraordinarily well. Anyone who has watched the impact-factor logic colonize a university, a hospital, or a research lab is reading Lyotard whether they know it or not.

title: Baudrillard: Simulacra and Hyperreality
description: The four orders of the image, and the disappearance of the real

concepts.title: From Sign to Simulacrum
concepts.contentHtml:
Jean Baudrillard begins as a sociologist of consumption (The System of Objects, 1968; The Consumer Society, 1970) and ends as the theorist of a culture in which signs have detached from any underlying reality. The pivotal text is Simulacra and Simulation (Simulacres et simulation, 1981), which opens with a faux-Ecclesiastes epigraph that he himself fabricated — a small joke that performs the book's thesis.

A simulacrum in Baudrillard's strict sense is not a copy of a real thing. It is a sign that no longer needs an original. The classical theory of representation assumed a chain: world → concept → sign. Baudrillard argues that under late capitalism, mass media, and digital reproduction, the chain has folded in on itself. Signs circulate without referents; the question "what is this image of?" becomes increasingly difficult to answer.

This is not merely a complaint about advertising. Baudrillard's wager is metaphysical: if the sign no longer points outside its own system, the very distinction between real and unreal — on which all classical realism depends — corrodes. "It is no longer a question of imitation, nor duplication, nor even parody. It is a question of substituting the signs of the real for the real."

concepts.title: The Four Orders of Simulation
concepts.contentHtml:
Baudrillard distinguishes four orders of the image, a historical sequence as much as a typology.

(1) Reflection — the image is a faithful representation of a reality (the Renaissance icon). (2) Perversion — the image masks and distorts a reality (ideology in the classical Marxist sense). (3) Mask of absence — the image masks the absence of a reality (the religious icon for an emptied-out theology). (4) Pure simulacrum — the image bears no relation to any reality whatever; it is its own pure simulacrum.

The fourth order is the postmodern condition. Baudrillard's notorious examples: Disneyland exists "to make us believe that the rest is real," when in fact Los Angeles and America are themselves of the order of hyperreal simulation. The Watergate scandal staged a moral order whose existence the scandal itself disproved.

You don't have to accept the strong claim that all postmodern signs are fourth-order to find the typology useful. It gives a vocabulary for what "reality TV," deepfakes, and synthetic financial instruments share: signs that simulate the conditions of a reality the underlying system no longer supplies.

concepts.title: Hyperreality and the Gulf War Provocation
concepts.contentHtml:
Hyperreality is Baudrillard's name for a regime in which simulations are more real than the real — sharper, more coherent, more affectively gripping than the messy actuality they replace. The Disneyland Mississippi steamboat is more "steamboat" than any working steamboat. The televised political debate is more "debate" than the policy disputes it putatively represents.

Baudrillard's most provocative application came in three short newspaper essays collected as The Gulf War Did Not Take Place (1991). The title is a deliberate scandal. He did not deny that bombs fell or that people died — a charge his critics often press in bad faith. He argued that the 1991 Gulf War, as received by Western publics, was a media event so thoroughly mediated by sanitized footage, video-game graphics, and Pentagon briefings that it failed to function as a war in any traditional sense: no enemy, no exchange, no symbolic violence — only one-sided technological administration packaged as live spectacle.

The strongest reading is diagnostic, not denialist: it indicts a media regime that delivers war as hyperreal entertainment. Subsequent decades — embedded journalism, drone footage, livestreamed conflict — have, if anything, made the diagnosis more urgent.

title: Jameson: The Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism
description: Pastiche, depthlessness, and postmodernism as a periodizing concept

concepts.title: Postmodernism as a Period, Not a Style
concepts.contentHtml:
Fredric Jameson's 1984 essay in New Left Review, expanded into Postmodernism, or, The Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism (1991), is the indispensable Marxist account of the postmodern. Jameson refuses to treat postmodernism as merely a style one might approve or reject. He treats it as the cultural dominant of a specific historical phase of capitalism.

He follows Ernest Mandel's three-stage model from Late Capitalism (1972): market capitalism, monopoly/imperialist capitalism, and the postwar multinational (or "late") capitalism of consumer goods, financialization, and global brands. Each stage has a corresponding cultural dominant — realism, modernism, postmodernism. Postmodern culture is what the third stage looks like from the inside.

This periodizing move is methodologically powerful. It immunizes Jameson against the objection that not every postmodern artwork shares one feature: the question is not whether a single feature defines all the work but whether a recognizable cultural system structures the field within which artists operate. It also keeps the political stakes legible: postmodernism is not a neutral style choice but the surface of an economic order one might still wish to contest.

concepts.title: Depthlessness, Pastiche, and the Waning of Affect
concepts.contentHtml:
Jameson catalogs the symptoms of postmodern culture with diagnostic precision. Depthlessness: the abandonment of the four hermeneutic depth-models that organized modernism — inside/outside, essence/appearance, latent/manifest (Freud), authenticity/inauthenticity (existentialism). What replaces them is the play of surfaces, the simulacrum.

The signature aesthetic mode is pastiche rather than parody. Parody mocks a style from a position outside it; pastiche imitates without that critical distance — "blank parody, parody that has lost its sense of humor." The famous comparison: Van Gogh's peasant shoes, charged with hermeneutic depth (toil, soil, world), versus Andy Warhol's Diamond Dust Shoes — flat, glittering, refusing to be read for hidden meaning.

The waning of affect follows: the alienated bourgeois subject of high modernism, capable of angst and depth-feeling, gives way to a fragmented, decentered subject for whom "feelings" are now "intensities" — free-floating euphorias and panics, no longer pinned to a deep self. Jameson links this, controversially, to Lacan's account of schizophrenia as a breakdown of the temporal chain of signifiers, producing a culture lived in a perpetual present.

concepts.title: The Bonaventure Hotel and Cognitive Mapping
concepts.contentHtml:
Jameson's most famous set-piece is his reading of John Portman's Bonaventure Hotel in downtown Los Angeles. Mirrored skin that refuses the city, entrances hidden from the street, an interior atrium so disorienting that pedestrians (Jameson reports) literally cannot locate themselves — the building stages, in concrete and steel, the new spatial regime of late capital. "Postmodern hyperspace... has finally succeeded in transcending the capacities of the individual human body to locate itself."

If postmodern culture induces this disorientation at the level of spatial and social cognition, the political task Jameson proposes is cognitive mapping: an aesthetic that would let the individual subject grasp her position within an unrepresentably large global system. The metaphor is Kevin Lynch's urban planning concept, applied to the totality of multinational capital. We don't yet have such an aesthetic, Jameson concedes; we may never. But the demand is what keeps his postmodernism political rather than merely descriptive.

The unresolved tension is whether cognitive mapping can survive the very conditions Jameson diagnoses. If depth-models have collapsed, on what surface does the map get drawn? This is the productive aporia at the heart of his project.

title: Rorty and the Liberal Ironist
description: Anti-foundationalism, contingency, and a postmodern pragmatism

concepts.title: After the Mirror of Nature
concepts.contentHtml:
Richard Rorty arrives at a postmodern position from inside analytic philosophy. His landmark Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature (1979) argues that the central tradition from Descartes to mid-century epistemology rests on a single picture: the mind as a mirror that, polished sufficiently, reflects reality accurately. Foundationalist epistemology is the project of inspecting the mirror.

Rorty marshals Quine on the analytic/synthetic, Sellars on the "myth of the given," Wittgenstein on language games, and Kuhn on paradigms to argue that the mirror metaphor cannot be salvaged. There is no theory-neutral access to a world that would adjudicate between vocabularies. What we call "truth" is what our peers — under appropriate epistemic norms — let us get away with saying.

This anti-foundationalism aligns Rorty with Lyotard and Derrida (whom he reads as fellow travelers), but his lineage is American pragmatism — Dewey above all, also James and the later Wittgenstein. Where Continental postmodernism is often elegiac, Rorty's tone is bracing and cheerful: the loss of foundations is a relief, not a catastrophe. Philosophy can stop being epistemology and start being a more open-ended conversation of mankind.

concepts.title: Contingency of Language, Self, and Community
concepts.contentHtml:
Contingency, Irony, and Solidarity (1989) develops the positive program. Rorty argues for three contingencies. The contingency of language: vocabularies are tools, not pictures; they are fashioned by historical accident, not delivered by reality. The contingency of selfhood: the self is a centerless web of beliefs and desires, redescribed across a life. (Here Rorty leans on Freud, Nietzsche, and the literary genealogies of Harold Bloom.) The contingency of liberal community: the values of liberal democracy — tolerance, expansion of solidarity, aversion to cruelty — are not grounded in human nature or rational necessity but in particular historical practices that we, as it happens, prefer.

Rorty borrows from Judith Shklar the dictum that liberals are people who think "cruelty is the worst thing we do." He notes that this commitment cannot be argued for from neutral premises — but neither can its opposite. Liberal politics rests on stories, sentiments, and the painstaking widening of the circle of "us," not on metaphysics.

The picture is a postmodernism that keeps its political nerve. Foundations are gone; that does not entail nihilism, only that we shoulder our commitments without metaphysical insurance.

concepts.title: The Liberal Ironist
concepts.contentHtml:
The book's signature figure is the liberal ironist. An ironist, in Rorty's stipulation, is someone who (i) has radical and continuing doubts about the final vocabulary she currently uses, (ii) realizes that argument in her current vocabulary cannot dissolve those doubts, and (iii) does not think her vocabulary is closer to reality than others. A liberal is someone who holds cruelty to be the worst thing we do.

The liberal ironist combines metaphysical homelessness with moral seriousness. She knows her vocabulary is contingent; she nevertheless cares passionately about the suffering of strangers. Solidarity, on this account, is built not by philosophical proof but by imagination — especially the imagination cultivated by novels (Dickens, Nabokov, Orwell) that let us feel cruelty from the inside of its victims.

Critics, including Rorty's friend Jürgen Habermas, charge that the position is privately corrosive (irony) and publicly hopeful (liberalism), and that the wall between the two cannot be maintained — that ironism, broadcast widely, would erode the very solidarity Rorty wants. Rorty replies that the wall is precisely a liberal achievement: keeping one's deepest doubts out of public deliberation, where they cannot help. Whether this division is psychologically stable or politically wise remains the live question.

title: Postmodern Aesthetics: Architecture, Fiction, Film
description: How the cultural diagnosis shows up in actual works

concepts.title: Architecture: Venturi and the Decorated Shed
concepts.contentHtml:
Postmodernism is most visibly a style in architecture. Robert Venturi's Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (1966) was the manifesto: against the high-modernist purity of Mies van der Rohe ("less is more"), Venturi proposed "less is a bore." Buildings should be hybrid, ambiguous, ornamented, drawing freely from history.

With Denise Scott Brown and Steven Izenour, Venturi extended the argument in Learning from Las Vegas (1972). The Strip, with its signs larger than the buildings they advertise, became a model. They distinguished the duck (a building whose form embodies its function — Long Island's actual giant duck) from the decorated shed (a generic structure with applied symbolic ornament). Postmodern architecture chose the shed: structure was honestly mundane, meaning was carried by the surface signage.

Realized examples: Philip Johnson's AT&T Building (1984), with its Chippendale broken pediment crowning a skyscraper; Michael Graves's Portland Building (1982); Charles Moore's Piazza d'Italia (1978) in New Orleans, an ironic Roman fragment. Charles Jencks famously dated the death of architectural modernism to 15 July 1972, 3:32 p.m. — the demolition of the Pruitt–Igoe housing project. The dating is a joke that nonetheless captures something: by the mid-1970s, the modernist program had visibly exhausted its credibility.

concepts.title: Fiction: Pynchon, DeLillo, Barth, and the Encyclopedic Novel
concepts.contentHtml:
In American fiction, postmodernism names a constellation: Thomas Pynchon (The Crying of Lot 49, 1966; Gravity's Rainbow, 1973), Don DeLillo (White Noise, 1985; Libra, 1988), John Barth ("The Literature of Exhaustion," 1967), Donald Barthelme, Robert Coover, Kathy Acker. Linda Hutcheon's A Poetics of Postmodernism (1988) coined historiographic metafiction for the dominant mode: novels self-consciously aware of their own fictionality while gripping real historical material.

Recurring features: encyclopedic sprawl mixing high and low culture; conspiracy as plot engine and epistemological metaphor; paranoia as the postmodern epistemic affect; references that fold back on the work itself; an unstable narrator who admits the writing of the book inside the book. Gravity's Rainbow stages V-2 rocketry, behaviorist psychology, Tarot, banana breakfasts, and Rilke quotations as one continuous text. White Noise renders the airborne toxic event as a media phenomenon before a chemical one.

The label "postmodern fiction" is contested; many of its supposed exemplars rejected it. But the family of strategies — metafictional self-awareness, pastiche of genre, paranoid plotting, depthless surfaces that nonetheless invite hermeneutic obsession — is a coherent literary phenomenon, and Jameson's diagnosis fits it remarkably well.

concepts.title: Film and Image: Pastiche, Citation, the Loss of the Outside
concepts.contentHtml:
Postmodern cinema is harder to define by formal rule than by sensibility. Jameson's own examples were the nostalgia film — Body Heat (1981), Chinatown (1974) — works that recreate the look of a past genre with such glossy fidelity that the past itself becomes a stylistic option rather than a lost reality. Subsequent canonical examples: Quentin Tarantino's pastiche of grindhouse and Hong Kong cinema; David Lynch's collapse of dream and waking diegesis; the Coen brothers' pastiche of noir and screwball; Blade Runner's Los Angeles assembled from Tokyo, ancient Egypt, and 1940s detective films.

The structuring feature is the loss of the outside. Modernist cinema (Godard, Antonioni, Tarkovsky) often worked by rupturing the diegetic surface to disclose something behind it — the apparatus, the political real, the metaphysical absence. Postmodern cinema increasingly refuses any such outside: the surface is all there is, and the pleasure is in tracking citation networks rather than excavating depth.

The political ambivalence is real. The same techniques can produce critical historiographic metafiction (Hutcheon's hopeful reading) or numbing depthless pastiche (Jameson's worry). The works themselves rarely settle the question; that ambiguity is a feature, not a flaw, of the postmodern aesthetic.

title: Critics from the Left, Right, and Center
description: Habermas, Eagleton, Hicks, and what they think postmodernism gets wrong

concepts.title: Habermas: Modernity Is Unfinished
concepts.contentHtml:
Jürgen Habermas's 1980 Adorno Prize address, "Modernity — An Unfinished Project" (Die Moderne — ein unvollendetes Projekt), is the locus classicus of the leftist critique of postmodernism. Habermas inherits the Frankfurt School project but resists its more pessimistic readings. Modernity, on his view, contains an emancipatory rational core — the Enlightenment's promise that public reason can underwrite both science and democratic legitimacy — and that promise is not yet exhausted.

Habermas's distinctive move is to relocate reason from the consciousness of the individual subject (Kant, Descartes) to the structure of communicative action: the unavoidable presuppositions of any genuine dialogue oriented toward understanding. When we make a sincere truth-claim, we implicitly commit to defending it with reasons all interlocutors could in principle accept. From these counterfactual presuppositions, Habermas reconstructs a discourse ethics capable of grounding democratic norms without metaphysical appeal.

Postmodernism, on this reading, throws the baby out with the bathwater. Lyotard and Derrida correctly diagnose the failure of subject-centered reason — but rather than reconstruct reason intersubjectively, they declare reason itself bankrupt. Habermas calls this move neoconservative in effect, since abandoning the rational standards of critique disarms the left and leaves market and bureaucratic systems unchallenged.

concepts.title: Eagleton: The Illusions of Postmodernism
concepts.contentHtml:
Terry Eagleton's The Illusions of Postmodernism (1996) sharpens the Marxist critique. Eagleton concedes that postmodernism captures something real about consumer culture and its dissolutions of identity. His complaint is that postmodernism mistakes its symptoms for its diagnoses: it celebrates fragmentation, plurality, and the death of the metanarrative as if these were political achievements rather than the cultural face of a particular phase of capital.

The political costs are concrete. If all metanarratives are equally suspect, then so is the metanarrative of class struggle — which is the only one with a serious analysis of what's wrong with the existing order. If "the subject" is merely a discursive effect, it becomes harder to speak coherently about exploitation, agency, or solidarity. Eagleton notes the irony: postmodern theory often arrives in academic life precisely as organized labor, working-class politics, and the welfare state are being dismantled. The vocabulary of "plurality" and "difference" is congenial to the very neoliberalism that is producing material immiseration.

The strongest version of the critique is not that postmodernism is wrong about everything — it has correctly registered the cultural texture of late capital — but that it is the wrong politics for that texture. The diagnosis is right; the prescription (irony, plurality, suspicion of universals) is precisely what late capital wants its theorists to deliver.

concepts.title: Hicks and the Right-Wing Critique
concepts.contentHtml:
From the right, the canonical book is Stephen Hicks's Explaining Postmodernism: Skepticism and Socialism from Rousseau to Foucault (2004). Hicks argues that postmodernism is a strategic intellectual response by socialism to its empirical defeat: with the failure of Marxist economic predictions and the moral collapse of the Eastern Bloc, the academic left turned from economic claims (which can be falsified) to discursive claims (which cannot). Postmodernism's anti-realism is, on this telling, less a philosophical conclusion than an ideological retreat.

Hicks traces a longer genealogy through Counter-Enlightenment thought — Rousseau, Herder, Fichte, Heidegger — claiming that postmodernism inherits an irrationalist tradition opposed to the Lockean-Enlightenment project. The book is hugely influential in popular online discourse and has shaped how a generation of right-wing intellectuals frames the academic humanities.

Academic specialists raise serious objections: Hicks reads major thinkers (Foucault, Derrida) selectively, conflates poststructuralism with postmodernism, and underweights the substantive philosophical arguments. Steelman the position regardless: there is a real question whether the timing of the postmodern turn — coinciding with the collapse of Marxism's economic credibility — is fully accidental, and whether anti-realist moves can do the political work their proponents want them to do. The diagnosis can be wrong in details and right in shape.

title: The Sokal Affair and the Science Wars
description: What a 1996 hoax did and didn't show

concepts.title: The Hoax
concepts.contentHtml:
In spring 1996, the cultural-studies journal Social Text published "Transgressing the Boundaries: Toward a Transformative Hermeneutics of Quantum Gravity," by Alan Sokal, a physicist at NYU. The article argued, with copious citations of Derrida, Lacan, Irigaray, and Latour, that physical reality is a social and linguistic construct, and that quantum gravity points toward a politically liberatory "postmodern science."

The same day, in the magazine Lingua Franca, Sokal revealed the article was a hoax. He had assembled it deliberately from buzzwords, philosophical solecisms, and outright nonsense — including the claim that the gravitational constant G is, like π, a historical-cultural variable. Social Text's editors had not had the article peer-reviewed by a physicist, and the issue was a special one on "Science Wars" intended to defend cultural studies against scientific critics.

The reception was a bonfire. Sokal and Jean Bricmont expanded the argument in Fashionable Nonsense (1997, French original Impostures intellectuelles), documenting what they called the systematic abuse of mathematical and physical concepts in works by Lacan, Kristeva, Irigaray, Baudrillard, Deleuze, Guattari, and Latour. The book remains the most cited single indictment of the genre.

concepts.title: What the Hoax Showed — and What It Didn't
concepts.contentHtml:
It is important to be precise about the hoax's actual entailments. The hoax decisively showed: (1) at least one prestigious cultural-studies journal had editorial standards too lax to detect a deliberate physics-flavored parody; (2) several canonical theorists had used technical mathematical and physical vocabulary in ways that, on careful inspection, were either incoherent or trivially metaphorical when taken to be doing real work.

The hoax did not show: (1) that all postmodern philosophy is nonsense — many central figures (Lyotard, Rorty, Jameson) are largely untouched by the specific charge; (2) that there is no legitimate field of social studies of science — Bruno Latour, Sandra Harding, and others have substantive arguments that survive the critique even when particular sentences don't; (3) that strong realism in philosophy of science is therefore vindicated. Sokal himself was careful about the scope: he was attacking specific abuses, not the entire humanities.

The honest reading: the hoax was a successful local operation that exposed real intellectual sloppiness and editorial laxity in a high-status corner of the humanities, while leaving the deeper philosophical questions about realism, social construction, and the authority of science exactly where it found them.

concepts.title: The Science Wars in Context
concepts.contentHtml:
The Sokal affair was one episode in the broader Science Wars of the 1990s. The combatants: on one side, sociologists and historians of science influenced by the Strong Programme in the sociology of scientific knowledge (David Bloor, Barry Barnes), by actor-network theory (Bruno Latour, Steve Woolgar — Laboratory Life, 1979), and by feminist epistemology (Sandra Harding, Donna Haraway). On the other, scientists and philosophers (Sokal, Steven Weinberg, Paul Gross, Norman Levitt — Higher Superstition, 1994) defending a more or less realist account of science.

The substantive question: how socially situated are the contents of scientific knowledge, not merely its institutions? A weak constructivism — "which problems get studied is shaped by funding, gender, politics" — is uncontroversial. A strong constructivism — "the truth of F = ma is itself a sociological achievement" — is hard to defend without sliding into incoherence (the strong version, applied reflexively, undermines its own claim to truth).

The most enduring legacies: a more sophisticated philosophy of science that takes social practice seriously without abandoning realism (Hacking, Cartwright, Kitcher), and a chastened cultural studies that more carefully distinguishes metaphorical uses of scientific vocabulary from claims about actual scientific content. The wars are formally over; their lessons are still being absorbed.

title: Self-Refutation and the Realist Reply
description: Boghossian, Searle, and the question whether postmodernism cuts its own throat

concepts.title: The Self-Refutation Charge
concepts.contentHtml:
The oldest objection to relativism, traceable to Plato's Theaetetus against Protagoras, is that it refutes itself. If "all truth is relative to a framework," then so is the claim that all truth is relative — in which case its assertion as a universal thesis is incoherent. The same objection, sharpened, comes for postmodernism: if every metanarrative is suspect, what about the metanarrative that every metanarrative is suspect? If there are no neutral standpoints, what is the standpoint of that claim?

Postmodern thinkers are aware of the worry; their replies vary. Lyotard insists his thesis is itself a local diagnosis, not a universal philosophical claim, and he cheerfully accepts the consequence that incredulity toward metanarratives is a position one can adopt or refuse — there is no neutral ground from which to compel it. Rorty grants that pragmatism cannot be argued for from outside any vocabulary; he recommends it on practical grounds.

Critics reply that this retreat to local, ironic, or pragmatic status saves the position only by emptying it. If postmodernism is just one local move among others, why does it implicate the rest of philosophy in its conclusions? The dialectic is genuinely difficult; "self-refutation" is rarely the simple knockout it advertises itself as.

concepts.title: Boghossian: Fear of Knowledge
concepts.contentHtml:
Paul Boghossian's Fear of Knowledge: Against Relativism and Constructivism (2006) is the most rigorous analytic-philosophical reply to the strong constructivist current in postmodern epistemology. Boghossian distinguishes three theses one might hold: (i) fact-constructivism (the facts themselves are socially constructed), (ii) knowledge-relativism (justification is always relative to an epistemic system), and (iii) rational explanation skepticism (rational considerations never explain why people hold beliefs).

Against fact-constructivism, Boghossian deploys a version of the standard incoherence argument: if every fact is a social construction, then so is the fact that every fact is a social construction, generating a vicious regress. He concedes a limited "description-dependent" constructivism (some facts depend on how we classify) but rejects its extension to physical reality.

Against knowledge-relativism, he argues that no clear formulation makes the position both stable and interesting: weak versions are trivial; strong versions are self-defeating. Against rational explanation skepticism (often associated with the Strong Programme), he argues it confuses sociological possibility with philosophical necessity. The book is the gold-standard analytic critique; it does not refute every postmodernist's actual view, but it sets the bar that those views must clear.

concepts.title: Searle and the Construction of Social Reality
concepts.contentHtml:
John Searle's The Construction of Social Reality (1995) supplies what is, in retrospect, the cleanest framing of the realism/constructionism dispute. Searle distinguishes brute facts (this stone weighs three kilos) from institutional facts (this piece of paper is a twenty-dollar bill). Institutional facts depend on collective intentionality — on us treating X as counting as Y in context C.

The framework is liberating. It concedes everything reasonable to constructivism — vast tracts of social life are socially constructed, including money, marriage, citizenship, gender roles, scientific institutions — without giving up brute facts about the physical world. The mistake of strong constructivism is to extend a thesis appropriate to institutional reality ("this is socially constructed") to brute reality, where it generates incoherence.

Most postmodernists, on a charitable reading, were always making the institutional point even when they spoke in stronger language. The interesting disputes therefore concern which facts are institutional and how thoroughgoing the institutional component is in regions traditionally treated as brute (the body? mental illness? the categories of physics?). Cleared of the strongest claims, postmodernism's enduring contribution is a sharpened attention to the institutional layer — a contribution analytic philosophy of social science has now substantially absorbed.

title: After Postmodernism
description: Metamodernism, the sincerity turn, and where the diagnosis stands now

concepts.title: Why "Post-Postmodernism"?
concepts.contentHtml:
By the late 1990s, postmodernism began to seem dated as a cultural dominant. Several developments pressed against its diagnosis. The internet collapsed the high/low distinction not by ironic pastiche but by sheer informational overflow. The 9/11 attacks reasserted, brutally, the priority of brute reality over its representations — Baudrillard wrote about this almost immediately in The Spirit of Terrorism (2002). Climate change made the loss-of-the-real diagnosis sound flippant. New literary voices (David Foster Wallace, Jonathan Franzen, Zadie Smith) explicitly thematized exhaustion with irony.

Wallace's 1993 essay "E Unibus Pluram: Television and U.S. Fiction" is the influential statement: irony, once a liberatory tool against bad-faith authority, has become the dominant mode of consumer culture itself, and a literature of irony can no longer distinguish itself from advertising. Wallace's call was for what he tentatively called the new sincerity — fiction willing to risk seeming naive, sentimental, or earnest in pursuit of unironic moral seriousness.

Whether "post-postmodernism" names a real successor or merely a reaction within postmodernism is contested. The case for a successor: irony is no longer felt as transgressive. The case against: every move ascribed to the new sincerity (self-aware sincerity, ironized earnestness) is exactly what postmodernism would predict.

concepts.title: Metamodernism and the Oscillation
concepts.contentHtml:
The most-cited candidate name for the successor sensibility is metamodernism, articulated by Timotheus Vermeulen and Robin van den Akker in their 2010 Journal of Aesthetics & Culture essay "Notes on Metamodernism." The diagnostic move is structural rather than thematic: metamodernism is not a synthesis of modernist sincerity and postmodern irony but an oscillation between them — alternately hopeful and skeptical, naive and knowing, never resting in either.

The cultural inventory includes Wes Anderson's films, Miranda July, the writing of David Foster Wallace and George Saunders, Olafur Eliasson's installations, and a wider "new sincerity" current in indie music and online discourse. The key feature: these works perform earnestness while remaining aware of its constructed nature, refusing both the modernist belief in sincerity-as-transparency and the postmodern dismissal of sincerity as kitsch.

The skeptical reply: "oscillation" is just the postmodern condition with a friendlier face. We never escaped postmodernism's premises (anti-foundationalism, the contingency of vocabularies); we have only become better at acting morally serious within them. On this reading, metamodernism is postmodernism that has stopped flagellating itself.

concepts.title: The Politicization of "Postmodern"
concepts.contentHtml:
Since roughly 2015, "postmodernism" has acquired a second life as a political epithet, particularly in right-of-center discourse where Jordan Peterson, Ben Shapiro, and others have repurposed Hicks's framing to identify postmodernism (often conflated with "cultural Marxism" and "critical theory") as the intellectual root of a broad set of contemporary cultural-political phenomena: identity politics, campus activism, transgender rights, antiracist pedagogy.

The genealogy is largely fictitious. The actual lineage of identity-political thought runs through Black feminist intellectual history (Kimberlé Crenshaw's intersectionality, 1989), critical race theory's legal scholarship (Derrick Bell, Patricia Williams), and disability studies — traditions independent of and often in tension with French postmodernism. Helen Pluckrose and James Lindsay's Cynical Theories (2020) argues for a closer connection ("applied postmodernism"); academic critics have pushed back hard.

The honest takeaway: "postmodernism" now means at least two distinct things — a recognizable late-twentieth-century intellectual formation studied here, and a much vaguer political-rhetorical bogey in 21st-century culture-war discourse. Conflating the two impoverishes both. Lyotard would have recognized the dynamic: the term has detached from its referent and become a sign in a new game, which is exactly what his theory predicted.
